title: The guide, closed
hookLine: tradition says the poet vanished mid-recital; the guide closes, and the last verse is a bow to the good friend
tomorrow: forty ways to meditate. how would you know which is yours?

lines: HE ROSE AND VANISHED, THEY SAY.
cards: Tradition tells a story about the first time this poem was heard.
At Nalanda, his monastery, some monks thought Shantideva did nothing but eat and sleep, so they asked him to recite in front of everyone, half hoping he'd fail. He began. He kept going.

And when he reached the chapter on wisdom, the story says, he rose into the air and vanished, while his voice went on. So, which verse would you keep, if the one reciting disappeared halfway? Readers answer differently.

teach.h: THE WISH, THE CONFESSION, THE WORK.
teach.b: Here's the guide, closed, in one breath. The wish to wake up for others. Confession: mend it now, because you'll leave it all behind.
Then the wisdom chapter you just walked through: two truths, looking for the body, looking for the self, not found, and wisdom that comes with warmth.
Then the dedication: for all, for the sick and afraid, for every road, as long as space remains. And the very last verse is a bow.

teach.h: A BOW TO THE GOOD FRIEND.
teach.b: Shantideva bows to Manjushri, by whose kindness, he says, his mind turned toward the good, and to the good friend, by whose kindness it grew.
A whole poem on living for others ends by thanking the ones who helped him. That's why it's called a guide and not a creed. It doesn't ask for a signature.
It asks to be used: on a hard shift, in a waiting room, at a delayed gate, in a fight you could let go of. The verse you keep is the one you'll reach for when the moment comes.

how: In Tibetan and other Mahayana communities the Bodhicaryavatara is taught chapter by chapter; some students keep a favorite verse to memorize and return to.

o: a list of beliefs a Buddhist has to accept
a rulebook monks must memorize before ordination
a poem on living for others, meant to be used

s: the story of Shantideva vanishing is told inside the poem
it's a story tradition tells about the poem, not part of it.
the guide ends with a bow to Manjushri and to the good friend
a poem on living for others ends by thanking those who helped.
the guide is a creed to sign more than a book to use

games.q: finals, a fight with your sister and a long shift, all this week. you can bring one verse. which kind fits the guide?
o: the one you'll actually reach for when the hard moment comes.
the longest one, so it covers every situation at once.
the one that sounds most impressive if someone asks.
games.why: a guide for living is meant for use. the verse you keep is the one that shows up on time.

practice: Let the verses of these weeks pass by, and keep the first one that stops you; don't overthink it. Then make a small plan: when this week will you need it?
Picture that moment, the room, the person, and the verse arriving right on time.

wordCard.voice: The guide: Shantideva's Bodhicaryavatara, a poem on living for others that ends with a bow to the good friend.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the title of Shantideva's guide, often rendered 'entering the way of awakening.'

carryVoice: Your line: a guide for living, meant for an ordinary Tuesday. Fifty of fifty, and the guide is closed.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 10.57–10.58 (the closing bows to Manjughosha/Manjushri and to the spiritual friend)
